sections.title: Inside a cell
sections.body: The nucleus contains DNA, which carries instructions for making proteins. Ribosomes assemble proteins. Many chemical reactions happen in the cytoplasm; mitochondria are the main site of aerobic respiration. The cell membrane controls movement into and out of the cell. Plant cells also have a cellulose wall, a permanent vacuole containing cell sap and, in photosynthetic tissues, chloroplasts.

sections.title: Bacteria and specialised cells
sections.body: Bacteria are prokaryotes: their DNA is not enclosed in a nucleus. They contain cytoplasm, a membrane and a cell wall, and may carry small DNA rings called plasmids. Specialised cells have structures suited to a job: sperm have a tail and many mitochondria; root hair cells have a large surface area for absorption. Not every plant cell has chloroplasts.

sections.title: Microscopes and scale
sections.body: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size. Convert both measurements to the same unit before dividing: 1 mm = 1,000 micrometres. Resolution is the ability to distinguish two close points. Electron microscopes resolve smaller structures than light microscopes. A clear biological drawing uses single outlines, accurate proportions and labels, rather than shading.

sections.title: Diffusion and osmosis
sections.body: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a higher concentration to a lower concentration. It is faster with a steeper concentration gradient, a higher temperature or a larger surface area. Osmosis is the net movement of water through a partially permeable membrane from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution. Water entering a plant cell helps make it turgid.

sections.title: Active transport and exchange
sections.body: Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient and requires energy transferred by respiration. Root hair cells can absorb mineral ions from dilute soil water this way. Thin exchange surfaces shorten the diffusion distance. Larger organisms have a smaller surface-area-to-volume ratio and need specialised exchange and transport systems.

sections.title: Division and stem cells
sections.body: Before mitosis, DNA is copied. Chromosomes are separated and the cell divides, producing two genetically identical daughter cells for growth, repair or asexual reproduction. Stem cells can divide and differentiate. Embryonic stem cells can form many cell types; adult stem cells have a more limited range. Consider benefits, rejection or tumour risks, and ethical arguments when evaluating treatment.

sections.title: Your board · microscopy
sections.body: Prepare a thin specimen on a slide, add a suitable stain and lower a coverslip carefully. Start with a low-power objective, focus, then increase magnification. Draw clear outlines and label visible structures. Magnification = image size ÷ real size; use the same units.

sections.title: Surface-area-to-volume reasoning
sections.body: A cube with side 1 has surface area 6 and volume 1: its ratio is 6:1. Doubling the side gives area 24 and volume 8, a ratio of 3:1. The decreasing ratio helps explain why diffusion alone becomes insufficient as organisms get larger.

practicals.title: Microscopy
practicals.method: Begin with low power, focus carefully and then increase magnification. Make a clear labelled drawing of visible structures. Measure the image and convert image and actual size to the same unit.
practicals.controls: Compare images at a known magnification. Distinguish increased image size from improved resolution.
practicals.example: A 30 mm image of a 0.05 mm cell has magnification 30 ÷ 0.05 = 600.
practicals.pitfall: Magnification is a ratio, not a length.

practicals.title: Osmosis in plant tissue
practicals.aim: Investigate how solution concentration affects water movement.
practicals.method: Compare equal-sized plant-tissue pieces in a range of solution concentrations. Record initial and final mass after the same time, blotting consistently before weighing. Repeat each concentration.
practicals.controls: Keep tissue source, dimensions, temperature, time and solution volume consistent.
practicals.example: A piece changes from 2.0 g to 2.3 g: percentage change = (0.3 ÷ 2.0) × 100 = +15%.
practicals.pitfall: Use initial mass as the denominator. At zero percentage mass change there is no net water movement.

actualCellQuestions.q: Give two differences between a bacterial cell and a typical animal cell.
actualCellQuestions.answer: Bacterial DNA is not enclosed in a nucleus. Bacteria have a cell wall; animal cells do not.
actualCellQuestions.explain: Award one point for each correct comparison. Bacteria can also have plasmids.

actualCellQuestions.subject: Biology
actualCellQuestions.q: A potato cylinder gains mass in distilled water. Explain why.
actualCellQuestions.answer: Water moves into its cells by osmosis through partially permeable membranes, from the more dilute external solution.
actualCellQuestions.explain: Link the direction of net water movement to the concentration difference.

actualCellQuestions.subject: Biology
actualCellQuestions.q: Root cells absorb ions from very dilute soil water. Explain why energy may be needed.
actualCellQuestions.answer: Ions may move against their concentration gradient by active transport, which requires energy from respiration.
actualCellQuestions.explain: The concentration gradient, rather than simply the size of an ion, explains the energy requirement.

actualCellQuestions.subject: Biology
actualCellQuestions.q: A cell image is 15 mm long. The real cell is 0.03 mm long. Calculate magnification.
actualCellQuestions.explain: 15 ÷ 0.03 = 500; magnification has no unit.

actualCellQuestions.subject: Biology
actualCellQuestions.q: Explain two ways a thin, folded exchange surface improves diffusion.
actualCellQuestions.answer: Folding increases surface area; a thin surface reduces diffusion distance.
actualCellQuestions.explain: Award one point for each structure linked to its effect.

actualCellQuestions.subject: Biology
actualCellQuestions.q: How do the chromosome numbers and genetic information of daughter cells produced by mitosis compare?
actualCellQuestions.answer: They normally have the same chromosome number and identical genetic information.
actualCellQuestions.explain: DNA is copied and the copies are separated before the cell divides.

actualCellQuestions.subject: Biology
actualCellQuestions.q: Give one potential benefit and one possible risk of using stem cells to replace damaged tissue.
actualCellQuestions.answer: They could replace lost specialised cells; uncontrolled division could form a tumour, or the tissue could be rejected.
actualCellQuestions.explain: A balanced answer links an application to a biological risk.

inheritanceReuse.title: DNA, genes and chromosomes
inheritanceReuse.body: DNA carries genetic information. A gene is a section of DNA associated with a functional product, often a protein. Chromosomes are long DNA molecules associated with proteins. The genome is all an organism’s genetic material. Different versions of a gene are called alleles.

inheritanceReuse.title: Sex chromosomes and inheritance
inheritanceReuse.body: Most human body cells have 23 pairs of chromosomes. The sex chromosomes are XX in females and XY in males in the simplified GCSE model. An egg carries an X chromosome; sperm may carry X or Y. A genetic cross gives an approximately equal probability of XX and XY offspring. Probabilities do not predict the sequence of births in a family.
